items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I think it’s the best jazz album I’ve heard since Bird and Diz.

ctx.x: What a wonderful — What’s in the immediate future for you? European tour?

Well I’m going on this tour. I’m getting together another album and I’m going to do a vocalese project. I’m going to lyricize and sing the Miles Davis “‘Round About Midnight” album. Yeah. That’s going to be a labor of love. I love that album. I think it’s the best jazz album I’ve heard since Bird and Diz.
Do you work at the piano when you do this?

items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: So when Bird came, somebody, it was my first wife, she said, “you know my husband scats and he’d like to scat with you.” So Bird said, “yeah, yeah, well send him up.” So I went up and they were doing “The Song Is You.”

ctx.x: Forget it, man, I’ve got 25 bucks.

But I couldn’t believe that and so I says whoa, man. So when I landed in Baltimore I immediately went to the nearest record shop and the guy told me where I could find Bird and Diz’s records. Because they weren’t sold in the respectable music shops. You had to go to the little dedicated jazz people to buy these records. So I bought as many of them as I could get my hands on and I bought anything that had to do with bebop, and bought Dave Lambert and Buddy Stewart. Because at that time in the store you could go in…
Kenny Dorham had just replaced Miles. So Bird had finished playing and he told me, so that I scatted. I scatted about ten choruses. I didn’t know when to stop. I was looking for a place to stop.

items.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So I walked up on the stage, and I scatted on The Song is You. He heard me make those Art Tatum changes, because that’s where he was from.

ctx.x: Did he ask you what you wanted to sing?

No. They played The Song is You, and he just – he motioned to me like that. So after Kenny Dorham got through – no, after he got through, he was motioning to me. So I walked up on the stage, and I scatted on The Song is You. He heard me make those Art Tatum changes, because that’s where he was from. After I was through, my knees were knocking. I was so nervous, I thought I was going to faint. All I wanted to do was get off that stage. Let me out of here. Because these cats, man – Tommy Potter, Max Roach, Al Haig…
Was that a milestone for you? How did that affect you?
